title: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For it follows as a simple corollary to this theorem of gnomons that we must not expect to find the logarithmic spiral manifested in a structure whose parts are simultaneously produced, as for instance in the margin of a leaf, or among the many curves that make the contour of a fish.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Gnomons and the time-element”. Scope: organic curves in general; accretionary hard parts versus soft tissues and leaf margins

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction contrasts observable structure classes and can be falsified by public morphology. Coverage is broad enough for a strong comparative test, although developmental mode must sometimes be assigned from external knowledge.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample curves from simultaneously formed soft outlines and incrementally accreted hard parts, fit logarithmic and rival models, and test association between accretion mode, logarithmic fit and visible growth lines. Credible logarithmic soft-tissue counterexamples would refute the exclusion.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Determining whether a part is formed simultaneously may require developmental knowledge.

Curve fitting is sensitive to landmark and scale selection.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is a contrast between two observable classes, and public images exist for shells, leaves and fish, with scans for many hard parts. Coverage is uneven for claws and tusks but sufficient to populate both sides of the contrast. Accepting or rejecting a logarithmic fit against alternative curves is a standard analysis.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit logarithmic spirals to accretionary hard parts (shell, tusk, horn, claw) and to structures built all at once (leaf margins, fish outlines). Better unique fits, usually with growth lines, in the first class, and poor fits in the second, support the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Claws and tusks are less densely archived than shells.

Some leaf margins and fin outlines can approximate a spiral over a short arc, so the test needs a pre-set fit criterion.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.85
